lines: A clean route out and a clean route back. I could ink that with a steady hand.
The gate is behind us and everyone is accounted for. Thank you.
I marked the whole route home in my head. You kept it clear.
I remember the relief of reaching a place with walls again.
You got me home without turning the journey into another disaster.
The first familiar face at the gate nearly made me laugh.
I slept through half the next day once I knew I was safe.
You checked the road ahead instead of pretending it was clear.
I noticed how often you looked back to make sure I was there.
The village seemed brighter after so long away.
The landmarks arrived in the order I hoped they would.
You stopped at the ridge long enough for me to fix our bearing.
We never had to choose between speed and leaving someone behind.
The last bridge held, the weather stayed clear, and nobody grew careless.
I knew we were safe when the village bell matched the mark on my map.
You let me check the return route before darkness made the choice for us.
We used fewer supplies than planned because the road stayed honest.
I have already corrected the one turn that nearly fooled us.
Every person who left appears on my list of those who returned.
That is the kind of journey I am willing to chart again.
That path needs a red mark on the map. I would rather not limp through it twice.
I made it home, but every red mark on that road now feels personal.
If we travel again, we plan the return before taking the first step.
I remember every step after the wound started hurting.
You slowed down when I could no longer hide the limp.
The road home felt twice as long once the bleeding began.
I was angry at my own weakness and took some of it out on you.
You kept checking the bandage even when I said it was fine.
I learned how heavy a small pack feels when you are hurt.
The first bed I saw looked better than any treasure.
The map did not show how far that hill would feel with a wound.
I measured the return in safe places to sit, not miles.
You found a gentler slope when I could no longer manage the marked path.
We left small blood marks at every stop. I do not care to retrace them.
The bridge was close on parchment and terribly far on foot.
I remember choosing the longer road because it stayed level.
My compass hand worked even when the rest of me did not.
The bandage held until the village roof appeared over the rise.
I have marked water and shelter along that route more carefully now.
Next time the return plan includes what happens when someone cannot walk quickly.
I can redraw a bad map. Redrawing trust is harder.
I followed your route because I trusted you. That trust did not survive it.
You stood close enough to guide me and chose to turn on me instead.
You promised a way home and led me into danger instead.
I trusted you until your plan stopped including my safety.
You knew more than you told me, and I paid for that silence.
I still wonder whether you expected me to survive.
The road was dangerous. Your dishonesty made it worse.
I came back with less trust than I left with.
You do not get credit for fixing trouble you chose to hide.
You changed the destination after I no longer knew the way back alone.
The route was yours, which made your silence feel deliberate.
I kept checking the map while the real danger walked beside me.
You used my trust as though it were another item in your pack.
Every warning makes sense now that I know what you withheld.
I will not follow a line drawn by someone who hides where it ends.
The road home gave me plenty of time to understand what you had done.
I have marked that place, but I will not mark you as safe again yet.
A wrong turn can be forgiven. Leading me wrong on purpose is different.
If we ever travel together again, I hold the map and choose the return.
I could chart that boat route. I might add a warning mark beside it.
The hull held together. I am less certain about the judgment behind the trip.
Open water carried us home after every landmark had disappeared.
I was glad to leave, but the boat did not feel like safety yet.
You kept us moving when the current tried to turn us around.
I watched the shore shrink and wondered if I had made a mistake.
The first night on the water felt longer than it was.
We rationed food because neither of us knew the true distance.
I learned to sleep through the sound of waves against wood.
You spotted land before I did.
I kept our bearing from the stars after the coast dropped away.
The current added distance that no straight line could explain.
We found the river mouth by watching the color of the water change.
Every island looked like the right one until we reached it.
You kept the bow steady while I checked the next landmark.
The map case stayed dry even when neither of us did.
I marked the reef from memory before sleep could blur its shape.
Our last stretch followed seabirds toward land and smoke toward home.
I know exactly where the wind forced us off the planned route.
The crossing deserves a better chart before anyone else attempts it.
